question:
In the homogeneous, isotropic single-layer case with y-uniform physical inputs, you observe
pronounced head differences between rows. Which responses are appropriate? (Select ALL correct
answers.)
success:
Correct. The intended symmetric problem admits a y-independent solution, so pronounced differences
between rows need investigation. Check the actual physical inputs and numerical convergence, and
examine more than one row. Agreement at one location does not establish that the entire spatial
field satisfies the expected symmetry.
error:
Not quite. Adding rows does not itself create a physical cause for north/south flow. Test the
intended symmetry across the domain and check the actual inputs and convergence before interpreting
row-to-row differences as hydraulic behaviour.

question:
With the same algorithm, converged 51 × 51 and 501 × 501 single-layer runs report the same number of
linear iterations. Which conclusions are valid? (Select ALL correct answers.)
success:
Correct. The total cell count increases by about 96.5 times, but an iteration on the larger system
generally involves more data and arithmetic. Timing also reflects implementation, memory access,
program overhead, and other work, so neither equal iteration counts nor the cell-count ratio alone
determines the measured runtime.
error:
Not quite. An iteration is not a fixed amount of work independent of grid size. Count the cells in
both horizontal directions, then distinguish iteration count, work per iteration, and the measured
elapsed time.

question:
You want to rank the three engine configurations using results from one two-dimensional case. Which
requirements support a defensible comparison? (Select ALL correct answers.)
success:
Correct. Performance comparisons require successful, sufficiently comparable solutions of the
intended problem. Record numerical settings and interpret residual norms rather than relying on
matching threshold numbers. Repeated timings help distinguish a reproducible difference from
variability, and iteration counts must retain their actual meanings.
error:
Not quite. A short failed run is not a successful solution, and equal threshold numbers do not
establish equal accuracy across different numerical criteria. Check the physical inputs, solution
quality, timing variability, and definitions of the reported counts.

question:
What distinguishes using random initial heads from introducing a random two-dimensional conductivity
field? (Select ALL correct answers.)
success:
Correct. Conductivity belongs to the physical model, whereas initial heads determine the numerical
starting point in this steady-state experiment. A two-dimensional conductivity realization can break
y symmetry. Keep that realization fixed when testing initial guesses, and measure whether a random
start helps or hinders convergence. Wetting restrictions may also affect which solution states are
accessible.
error:
Not quite. Ask whether the changed input belongs to the steady-state hydraulic problem or to its
numerical initialization. Change one factor at a time, preserve the actual conductivity array, and
avoid assuming that randomness necessarily makes a starting estimate worse.

question:
The current uniform-head control allows 0.1 m but not exactly 0.0 m. With bottom 0 m and positive
CHD heads, which conclusions about a low-start experiment are justified? (Select ALL correct
answers.)
success:
Correct. The available near-bottom trial does not establish the outcome of an unsupported exact-zero
trial. Positive CHD heads remain imposed, so an argument that transmissivity must be zero everywhere
is not valid. The response to an exact-zero interior guess depends on the numerical formulation,
accessible wetting transitions, and the hydraulic connections and sources.
error:
Not quite. Separate the permitted 0.1 m experiment from a hypothetical exact-zero start, and keep
the CHD heads distinct from interior guesses. Do not infer universal failure from interior saturated
thickness alone without considering the boundaries and the engine's wetting treatment.

question:
You plan staged three-dimensional tests under the app's 255,000-cell cap. Which statements and
practices are appropriate? (Select ALL correct answers.)
success:
Correct. The 51 × 51 cases contain 7,803 cells with three layers and 26,010 with ten. The optional
159 × 159 × 10 case contains 252,810 cells; 501 × 501 × 10 would contain 2,510,010. A case fitting
the cap is not automatically practical to run. Increase complexity in stages and judge numerical and
hydraulic results alongside runtime.
error:
Not quite. Multiply all three dimensions before comparing a grid with the cap. Distinguish an
admissible cell count from a practical or accurate computation. Use the smaller staged calculations
to inspect convergence and hydraulic behaviour before considering the optional larger case.
